references.text: Isaiah prophesied about the Messiah that the Lord's Spirit would rest upon him, and that he would not judge by what his eyes see. The mockers' demand that Jesus 'prophesy' who struck him is an ironic twist on his prophetic gift. [ref: Isa 11:2-3|Isaiah 11:2-3]

Isaiah's suffering servant was despised and forsaken, beaten and mistreated. The scene where Jesus is covered, struck, and mocked is a direct fulfillment of the prophecy about the suffering servant. [ref: Isa 53:3-5|Isaiah 53:3-5]
Matthew's parallel account describes the same event where they spat in Jesus' face, struck him, and asked him to prophesy who had hit him. [ref: Matt 26:67-68|Matthew 26:67-68]
Mark's parallel account tells that they covered his face, struck him with their fists, and asked him to prophesy. [ref: Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65]

The Lord's servant in Isaiah gave his back to those who struck him, and his cheeks to those who pulled out his beard; he did not hide his face from shame and spitting. Jesus' suffering in this scene reflects this prophecy. [ref: Isa 50:6|Isaiah 50:6]
Micah prophesied that the ruler of Israel would be struck on the cheek with a rod, pointing forward to the abuse Jesus endured. [ref: Mic 4:14|Micah 4:14]
The preceding verse provides the immediate context: the men holding Jesus captive began to mock and strike him before covering his face and demanding that he prophesy. [ref: Luke 22:63|Luke 22:63]
Also in John's account, Jesus was struck during the interrogation, and Jesus responded by challenging the justice of the action. [ref: John 18:22-23|John 18:22-23]
